Which team is more likely to force the other into turnovers at decisive moments?
A) Arkansas’s pace-and-pressure system plus length/anticipation will create enough ball disruption to break Hawaii’s veteran execution.
B) Hawaii is relatively ball-disciplined enough in execution and Arkansas’s style won’t translate well into consistent turnover generation; Arkansas’s own low turnovers (9.0/game) limits Hawaii’s opportunity.

Referee whistle/physicality factor: Will the officiating lead to a relatively low free-throw disparity (a “let them play” game) rather than a whistle-heavy game?
A) Yes. Fouls are relatively controlled; the free-throw disparity stays small, keeping the game closer to a possession-defense/rebounding contest.
B) No. The officiating becomes whistle-heavy enough that free throws create a large scoring swing, and the team that attacks the line more wins that lever (likely Arkansas given their FT volume).

Does recent form/trajectory at the end of the season reduce upset risk for Arkansas or for Hawaii?
A) Arkansas momentum—Arkansas enters the bracket on strong form (8–2 last 10; five-game winning streak), suggesting the star system is peaking and the team handles high-leverage moments well.
B) Hawaii momentum—Hawaii is also riding late confidence (Big West tournament champ) and has repeatedly executed in close games (buzzer beaters, clutch free throws), indicating a psychological edge in one-possession scenarios.

In projected game conditions, which team has the edge in effective scoring efficiency (eFG%)?
A) Arkansas—Arkansas’s offense is efficient enough in high-leverage looks (52.2% eFG on the accessible metric; plus .500 FG and .389 3P%) that it wins the efficiency matchup even when Hawaii defends at an elite level.
B) Hawaii—Hawaii’s defense suppresses opponent eFG (opponents eFG% .438 vs Hawaii per Sports-Reference), and since Hawaii’s own offense is not highly dependent on elite shooting variance, it can keep Arkansas’s realized efficiency low in a half-court contest.

Will Arkansas get to the free-throw line at a rate that meaningfully surpasses Hawaii’s ability to keep fouls down (i.e., Arkansas attempts a materially larger number of FTs)?
A) Yes. Arkansas attempts substantially more free throws than Hawaii (not just marginally—enough to be a visible efficiency lever).
B) No. Arkansas’ free-throw attempts are not meaningfully higher than Hawaii’s (or Hawaii gets as many/more attempts), removing a key Arkansas scoring pathway.

Will Arkansas’s turnover total stay at or below its season typical level (about 9.0 turnovers/game)?
A) Yes — Arkansas commits ~9 or fewer turnovers, preserving its high assist/organization and preventing Hawaii from converting mistakes into run-outs.
B) No — Arkansas’s turnovers rise meaningfully above its typical level (because of pressure/length/handling), creating transition opportunities for Hawaii and increasing volatility.

Does coaching adaptation most plausibly favor the higher-variance rematch/adjustment style (Calipari) or the game-to-game veteran correction style (Ganot)?
A) Calipari advantage—Arkansas will implement in-game and between-game adjustments that specifically target Hawaii’s biggest pressure points (route the offense away from contested paint touches, attack spacing matchups, and manage fouls/boards), because Arkansas has shown clear tactical flips after losses (e.g., Auburn rematch; Texas after Florida).
B) Ganot advantage—Hawaii’s staff will adjust its containment/spacing and defensive assignment to match Arkansas’s star-driven pressure, based on documented season splits vs UC San Diego (10-point output swing) and quick resets after ugly losses (wins immediately after the Long Beach State defeat).

Will the game be decided primarily by half-court execution rather than transition scoring margin?
A) Yes — the transition/free-break split is relatively small; half-court possessions and set execution decide the outcome.
B) No — transition (or fast-break scoring created from stops/boards) becomes a major margin driver for one team.

How important is Arkansas’s three-point attempt volume/rhythm for avoiding upset vulnerability?
A) Arkansas’s moderate 3PA rate is fine because they can generate enough rim/FT/second chances; they do not require high three-point volume to win.
B) Arkansas’s success depends on being able to hit threes at key moments; when opponents wall the lane, Arkansas becomes ordinary and can lose if 3PT variance goes against them.

Which team’s offense is more likely to get efficient shot quality against the other’s half-court defense?
A) Arkansas will get paint pressure and high-quality rim/short-2 looks despite Hawaii’s rim protection and rebounding structure.
B) Hawaii’s contain-and-finish defense (holding opponents to low opponent eFG/.411 FG and .304 3P%) will force Arkansas into lower-efficiency jump shots and fewer paint touches.

Who is more likely to win the free-throw scoring edge?
A) Arkansas’s attack generates a larger free-throw volume/attempt rate (794 FT attempts in 34 games) and will outscore Hawaii at the line.
B) Hawaii’s half-court pressure and late-clock execution creates more attempts/makes (802 FT attempts, 18.6 makes per game; top-35 in FT makes/attempts), swinging free throws in Hawaii’s favor.

Does the most plausible matchup path rely on Arkansas controlling paint/boards, or on Hawaii neutralizing paint efficiency and winning rebound battles? (Historical/situational style of win-condition)
A) Arkansas win path—Arkansas will follow its proven template: paint pressure plus rim protection and second-shot creation (Ewin/Brazile finishing; offensive rebounding strength), which has been effective vs strong opponents despite occasional board losses.
B) Hawaii win path—Hawaii wins by defending eFG/3P% at an elite rate and protecting the defensive glass/limits foul charity, so Arkansas’s interior pressure ends up producing lower-quality looks and Hawaii outlasts with a defensive possession war.

Does the Arkansas offense’s turnover/ball-protection profile meaningfully limit Hawaii’s defensive disruption?
A) Yes—Arkansas averages only 9.0 turnovers per game with a 1.9 assist/turnover ratio, which supports the claim that Hawaii won’t be able to create enough transition points to swing the game.
B) No—Hawaii’s defense forces tough possessions and Arkansas’s style (paint pressure + drives + ball-screen sequences) can still create live-ball turnovers/errant passes; the matchup produces a turnover differential that benefits Hawaii (i.e., Arkansas is disrupted more than its season turnover rate suggests).

A) Yes. Hawaii’s size/rim protection reduces Arkansas’ paint/inside scoring efficiency (fewer made shots or lower FG% in the lane).
B) No. Arkansas still converts enough inside/paint opportunities (paint efficiency holds up), limiting Hawaii’s rim-protection impact.

A) Arkansas wins the rebounding battle (including meaningfully more offensive rebounds), limiting Hawaii second chances and generating extra possessions.
B) Hawaii wins the rebounding battle (including more defensive rebounds and more second-chance opportunities), keeping Arkansas from converting rim pressure into efficient looks and possessions.

A) Arkansas gets the larger free-throw attempt edge (consistent with its season’s high FT volume), keeping them ahead even if field-goal efficiency fluctuates.
B) Hawaii prevents Arkansas from getting to the line at a meaningful rate (closer to Hawaii’s defense strength: disciplined, limited fouling/low opponent FT-rate), reducing Arkansas’ variance cushion and making the game more shooting/rebounding dependent.

Will Arkansas’s rim protection (blocks/length) be enough to change Hawaii’s shot selection volume (especially near the basket)?
A) Arkansas’s 5.1 blocks/game and rim erase ability will reduce easy paint scoring, forcing Hawaii into less efficient midrange/jump shooting.
B) Hawaii’s size and interior anchor will still generate efficient attempts; Arkansas’s rim defense will contest but not fully prevent Johnson’s production and paint touches.

How predictive is Hawaii’s recent upset/close-game success versus a stronger opponent?
A) Hawaii’s repeated one-possession wins show transferable mental toughness and late-game execution that can upset a higher-ranked team.
B) Those close wins may be inflated by weaker scheduling; vs an elite SEC-level creator like Acuff, Hawaii’s half-court offense may run out of margin.

Can Arkansas force Hawaii into a faster, less-controlled pace than Hawaii prefers?
A) Yes — Arkansas’s transition creation and tempo management raise the effective pace and reduce Hawaii’s ability to run its half-court rebounding/contain plan.
B) No — Hawaii keeps possessions in controlled half-court segments (pace roughly neutral or slower), turning the game into a grind where its defense/rebounding dominates.

A) Arkansas—Arkansas’s frontcourt shot-blocking/finishing options (Brazile, Ewin) and guard creation (Acuff + Thomas secondary scoring) reduce dependence on any single player staying clean, making it easier to maintain quality even with rotation volatility.
B) Hawaii—Hawaii’s size-and-rebounding rotations (multiple 6-8/6-9/6-10 forwards plus a shot-blocking center) mean it can sustain interior defense and rebounding effectiveness even when matchups shift, because depth supports maintaining the defensive identity.

Neutral-site/context factor: does either team receive a meaningful home-court-like advantage via travel/rest or venue conditions (e.g., closer fans, familiarity, travel)?
A) Yes. Arkansas has an operational advantage (less travel disruption / better game-day conditions), supporting consistent shooting and defensive intensity.
B) No. Neither team has an appreciable contextual edge; both teams operate under similar rest and environment conditions, so on-court matchups dominate.

Which team creates more opponent turnovers in this specific game (and turns those into points)?
A) Arkansas creates a higher turnover rate for Hawaii and converts those mistakes into transition/quick scoring, overpowering Hawaii’s grind defense.
B) Hawaii limits turnovers enough and disrupts Arkansas’ ball progression so that Arkansas does not generate a transition advantage; instead, Hawaii’s possessions remain relatively controlled and Arkansas’ assist/turnover advantage doesn’t translate into points.

How much will Arkansas’ offensive efficiency be suppressed when forced into more half-court, low-paint-visit possessions by Hawaii’s size/contain defense?
A) Arkansas maintains strong half-court efficiency (e.g., scoring near its season average) despite Hawaii’s length and defensive structure, because Acuff and the screening/finishing menu remain productive.
B) Arkansas’ efficiency drops substantially in half-court (more low-quality jump shots and fewer paint/dive/transition finishes), because Hawaii credibly packs and contests the lane and takes away the drive-and-finish lanes.

Will Arkansas control the paint enough that Hawaii receives fewer than their typical number of shots at the rim (as reflected by opponent two-point attempts close at the rim)?
A) Yes. Hawaii’s opponents’ shot profile against Arkansas would show fewer high-efficiency looks at/below the rim for Hawaii relative to Arkansas’ norms (i.e., Arkansas limits rim-quality offense).
B) No. Hawaii sees a rim/paint-heavy shot profile and gets more high-quality interior looks than Arkansas’ typical opponents would allow.

Will either team’s three-point attempt volume diverge from its typical season profile enough to swing the matchup (Arkansas at ~0.389 made-3s; Hawaii more balanced ~31.5% ORtg profile)?
A) Arkansas gets unusually high three-point effectiveness/volume compared to its typical profile (or Hawaii is forced into fewer makes), producing a spread-out advantage.
B) Neither side gets an outlier perimeter outcome; shooting remains near expected ranges, making rebounding/FTs/defense decide the game.
